To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the mRNAs for the neuropeptides TRH, ENK, and NPY are differentially altered in the limbic system of rats following an amygdaloid kindled seizure.
Neuropeptide mRNAs were transiently increased in limbic structures following an amygdaloid kindled seizure.
the expression of mRNAs encoding neuropeptides that may have anticonvulsants or proconvulsants effects are increased in limbic brain regions after a seizure.

understanding the role of peptides in epilepsy and their possible role in the treatment of epilepsy.
identifying the molecular mechanisms of seizure induced plasticity.
the mechanisms by which neuropeptides may be involved in the regulation of seizure activity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neuropeptide mRNA levels are altered in the dentrate gyrus, and the pyriform and entorhinal cortices.
the expression of neuropeptide genes is altered in a non-uniform manner and with a complex time course in response to an amygdala seizure, and these changes are regionally and time dependent.

TRH and NPy mRNAs are increased in the dentrate gyrus granule cells and pyriform cortex 4 h after the seizure and return to normal by 24 h, whereas ENK mRNA is elevated in the pyriforn and entorhinal cortex at 4 and 2 h after the seizure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the amygdala plays an important role in the control of the expression of these neuropeptide genes in the hippocampus.

the neuropeptides TRH, ENK and NPY are differentially regulated in limbic brain regions following a seizure and that these alterations in gene transcription may be important in understanding both the anticonvulsants and proconvulsant actions of these neuropeptide systems.
the neuropeptides, TRH and ENK, have a transient anticonvulsent effect, whereas NPY and TRH have a long term, proconvulsant effect.

the neuropeptides, which are released from neurons, can have both anticonvulsants and proconvulsant actions.
